Kanji Radicals Guide: 30 Common Forms and Components

Kanjidon Team · Jan 30, 2026

Kanji becomes easier to inspect when you can name recurring parts. But two ideas are often blurred together: a dictionary radical is the component used to classify a character, while a visual component is any recurring form you use to analyse or remember it. This guide introduces 30 useful forms without claiming that they decode every character or replace vocabulary study.

Radicals and Components Are Not the Same Thing

In traditional lexicography, a character is assigned one indexing radical. The classic Kangxi system contains 214 classification radicals. A character can also contain several other visual or phonetic components, and modern teaching systems may give those pieces memorable names. Calling every piece a radical is convenient in study apps, but it is not a precise statement about dictionary classification or historical formation.

What Components Can Tell You

  • A recurring form can help you distinguish similar characters.
  • Some components provide a broad semantic cue: 氵 often appears in characters connected with water or liquids.
  • Some components provide a historical sound cue, although modern pronunciation changes mean the clue is not always transparent.
  • Position can change a form: 水 may appear as 氵, 人 as 亻, and 手 as 扌.
  • A mnemonic is a memory aid. It should not be presented as the true origin of a character unless an etymological source supports it.

Three Examples of Productive Analysis

Water: 水 and 氵

The left-side form 氵 appears in 海 (sea), 河 (river), 洗 (wash) and 泳 (swim). That shared cue can help you group the shapes, but it does not give you each word's reading. Learn the component and the vocabulary together.

Person: 人 and 亻

The side form 亻 appears in 休 (rest), 住 (reside) and 体 (body). A learner might remember 休 as a person beside a tree, but that image is a mnemonic, not a complete etymological explanation.

Hand: 手 and 扌

The side form 扌 occurs in 持 (hold), 打 (strike) and 押 (push). It can suggest an action involving the hand, while the remaining component helps distinguish the character.

A Practical Study Routine

  • Notice recurring forms inside a kanji you are already learning.
  • Check which part is its dictionary radical if you need to look it up.
  • Attach a short memory cue only when the shape is difficult to retain.
  • Learn one or two real words so the kanji has a reading and context.
  • Contrast look-alikes instead of assuming that a shared component guarantees a shared meaning.
  • Review the complete word through retrieval and reading, not component labels alone.

What the Number 214 Means

The number 214 refers to the Kangxi radical classification inherited by many dictionaries. It is not a kanji alphabet, and learners do not need to memorize the entire set before beginning. Other dictionaries and digital systems can organize characters differently. Use the classification as a lookup tool and components as analysis tools.
